title: The Pipeline Idea, and Reading the Space-Time Diagram
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Stages, Timing and Speed-up
quickIdea: Pipelining cuts one instruction's trip through the datapath into stages and lets different instructions sit in different stages in the same cycle. A k-stage pipeline then finishes one instruction per cycle in the steady state, instead of one every k cycles.
remember: Five classic stages: IF (fetch the instruction), OF or ID (decode and read the registers), EX (ALU work, address arithmetic, branch test), MA or MEM (data memory), RW or WB (write the register).
A pipeline diagram has one row per instruction and one column per clock cycle, and every row is shifted one column to the right of the row above it.
Latency does not improve: one instruction still occupies k cycles, plus the latch time. Throughput improves: after the fill, one instruction leaves the pipeline every cycle.
A stall is drawn as a gap in a row, or as a bubble occupying a stage; the total time is the number of columns, so count columns rather than trusting a formula.
With n instructions, k stages and no stalls the total is k + n - 1 cycles; the first k - 1 cycles are the fill and the last k - 1 the drain.

example.prompt: A 5-stage pipeline runs 8 instructions with no stalls. How many cycles does it take, and how many would the same 8 take on the unpipelined machine at the same clock?
example.work: Pipelined: k + n - 1 = 5 + 8 - 1 = 12 cycles, because the first instruction takes 5 cycles and each of the other 7 adds one. Unpipelined, each instruction must pass through all five stages in sequence, so 8 x 5 = 40 cycles.
example.answer: 12 cycles against 40, a speed-up of 40/12 = 3.33. It is well short of the ideal 5 because on a program this short the fill and drain are a large part of the total.

gateAngle: Every pipeline question is a diagram question. GATE CSE 2021 Set 1 Q.53 hands you five stage delays and a latch delay and asks for the time of 100 instructions: the answer is 104 columns of 165 ns, that is 17160 ns. GATE CSE 2013 Q.45 asks for the same thing with a branch in the middle, and the answer is 15 columns of 11 ns.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does pipelining raise throughput but not the latency of a single instruction?
variations.why: It separates the two quantities a beginner tends to merge, and it is the sentence GATE's definition questions are built on.
variations.answer: Because the stages of one instruction are still traversed one after another: the fifth stage of an instruction cannot start before its fourth has finished, so a lone instruction still needs k clock cycles. What changes is that the stage left idle behind it is now used by the next instruction, so k instructions are in flight at once and one finishes per cycle.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A 6-stage pipeline with 1 ns stages runs 10 instructions with no stalls. How many cycles and what speed-up over the unpipelined machine at the same clock?
variations.why: It moves the same reasoning to a different k and n, which is exactly how the exam varies the 2021 question.
variations.answer: 6 + 10 - 1 = 15 cycles; unpipelined 10 x 6 = 60 cycles; speed-up 60/15 = 4, against an ideal ceiling of 6.

trap.what: Saying that pipelining makes an instruction faster.
trap.why: An instruction still needs every stage; pipelining overlaps different instructions, not the stages of one instruction. A single instruction is not speeded up at all, and is slightly slowed by the latch delay.
trap.counterexample: One instruction alone on a 5-stage, 1 ns-per-stage pipeline takes 5 cycles (more, with latches), exactly as on the unpipelined machine. The gain appears only from the second instruction onward.

check.question: A 4-stage pipeline runs 20 instructions. How many cycles does it need, and in which cycle does the first instruction finish?
check.answer: 4 + 20 - 1 = 23 cycles, and the first instruction finishes at the end of cycle 4.
check.explanation: The fill is k - 1 = 3 cycles before the second instruction can start leaving, so the total is n + k - 1 and the first completion is at cycle k.
